candidates.attacker_control:
The filter-xml module is the XML import/conversion framework: XMLInputFilterFactory ("filter+xml", 'Generates wiki events from generic XML file') and the other XML input filters feed document content into DefaultXMLParser via DefaultXMLParserFactory, and the wire format is exactly the one produced by DefaultXMLSerializer (which itself writes the parameter-type attribute for Object-typed parameters, DefaultXMLSerializer.java:338-343). An XML document supplied for such a conversion controls the event/parameter names and the parameter-type attribute value, e.g. a known filter event containing

...

(default XMLConfiguration names: block/p/n/t). The attacker therefore selects the Java class that the server loads, instantiates and populates. For the job path, the deserialized XML is the on-disk status file, so attacker control there depends on being able to influence/replace a status file.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The parameter-type attribute is part of the intended filter XML format (DefaultXMLSerializer writes it for Object-typed parameters), so the parser accepting it is by design - the defect is that no allowlist/type restriction is applied to attacker-supplied values. However, the same 'no XStream security framework' design is explicitly acknowledged and left in place in SafeXStream (TODO comment) and NoWarningXStream (warning suppression), so this is not merely an unused API. XStream 1.4.17 without setupDefaultSecurity/permissions does not block arbitrary types (it only logs a warning, which NoWarningXStream suppresses). I could not verify, from this repository alone, a specific end-to-end UI/REST path that feeds untrusted XML to the filter parser (imports/migrations may be admin-gated), nor prove that a concrete gadget class exists on a given deployment classpath, so this remains a lead rather than a confirmed exploitable vulnerability. Competing explanations for the same sinks (e.g. that only trusted, server-generated status files are ever read) were considered but cannot be established from the provided sources.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary class initialization (static initializers run because Class.forName uses initialize=true), arbitrary object instantiation and reflective field population from attacker-supplied XML. With a suitable class/gadget chain on the classpath this is a remote-code-execution primitive (deserialization gadget) with full server compromise; at minimum it allows attacker-directed object construction/class loading, which can cause file writes, SSRF/JNDI-style side effects or denial of service, i.e. loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of the wiki.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The server must parse XML with the filter module (wiki/XAR import or migration, FilterStreamConverterJob, or any other caller of XMLParserFactory/ParameterManager) OR read an attacker-influenced job status / extension history XML file. 2) The XML must name an element/parameter known to the listener's FilterDescriptor (any known parameter suffices, since the type attribute overrides the declared type). 3) A usable class/gadget must exist on the deployment classpath; XStream 1.4.17 is used without any permission framework (pom.xml xstream.version 1.4.17), so no type is blocked by default.
candidates.root_cause: xwiki-commons deserializes XML with XStream while relying on no type restrictions at all. (1) In the filter module, DefaultXMLParser.unserializeParameter() takes the parameter's class from the XML attribute that names the parameter type (default "t") and loads it with Class.forName(typeString, true, TCCL) before handing the element to the ParameterManager; XStreamParameterManager then unmarshals the element with a plain ParameterXStream/NoWarningXStream instance that never enables the XStream security framework (no allowTypes/permissions/whitelist), and for empty parameter elements org.xwiki.filter.xml.internal.XMLUtils.emptyValue() calls newInstance() on the attacker-chosen class. (2) In the job module, JobStatusSerializer reads status XML with SafeXStream, whose initialize() deliberately leaves the XStream whitelist disabled (setupDefaultSecurity commented out because "the default setup is to use a white list which is totally unusable for job serialization"), i.e. arbitrary type instantiation during fromXML.
candidates.title: Unrestricted XStream deserialization of attacker-influenced XML with attacker-selected class in xwiki-commons (filter XML parser and job-status XStream wrapper)
candidates.trace:
Untrusted XML -> AbstractXMLInputFilterStream/XMLInputFilterFactory (XMLInputFilterStreamUtils.createXMLEventReader) -> DefaultXMLParserFactory.createParser -> DefaultXMLParser.endElement() collects

children (lines 455-474) -> setParameter() (lines 298-328) resolves the declared parameter -> unserializeParameter() (lines 364-373) reads the 't' attribute and executes Class.forName(typeString, true, Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader()) -> XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize() (lines 110-127) calls xstream.unmarshal(new DomReader(element), null, dataHolder) on a ParameterXStream that extends NoWarningXStream, which extends XStream without any security framework and even overrides unmarshal() to suppress the "Security framework ... not initialized" warning -> XStream instantiates the attacker-selected class and sets its fields reflectively; for an empty element, XMLUtils.emptyValue() calls clazz.newInstance() directly (filter-xml XMLUtils lines 109-124). In parallel, JobStatusSerializer.read() (lines 137-151) calls SafeXStream.fromXML() on the stored status, with the type whitelist intentionally disabled in SafeXStream.initialize() (lines 80-86).
candidates.unverified: Runtime reachability from a low-privileged user (platform-side callers of the filter-stream framework are not in this repository); existence of a working gadget chain in a real deployment classpath; whether the XAR/instance XML configuration in practice exposes a known parameter name usable with the type attribute; whether job status / extension history files can be attacker-influenced in a deployed XWiki (the status file path assumption is unverified); no code execution or test run was performed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (with CWE-470 externally-controlled class selection)

coverage_summary: get_source_scope reports 1424 model-visible files (1186 Java) with no sensitive-path/symlink exclusions and a binary-content filter (NUL byte in first 8 KiB). There are no test sources in the snapshot (only main sources and build files), and the P1 relation index (get_relation_scope) is explicit that it is syntax/name-based only: 1423/1424 files indexed (1 missing), 3 parse errors, no control-flow, no data-flow, no semantic resolution, Spring annotation-name candidates only - so index facts were used purely for navigation and every candidate edge was checked against source text. I reviewed module structure and the security-relevant code paths in xwiki-commons-xml (XMLUtils, DefaultXMLReaderFactory, LocalEntityResolver, HTML cleaner/sanitizer), xwiki-commons-xstream (SafeXStream and converters), xwiki-commons-job (DefaultJobStatusStore, JobStatusSerializer), xwiki-commons-filter (XML parser/parameter XStream, input streams, job requests), xwiki-commons-netflux (endpoint, channel/user/key generation), xwiki-commons-extension (serializer/storage/repositories, path encoding), xwiki-commons-velocity (sandbox/introspectors), classloader, crypto, cache-infinispan and websocket modules, plus repository-wide searches for DocumentBuilderFactory/SAXParser/XMLInputFactory, XStream/ObjectInputStream/readObject, Class.forName/newInstance, Runtime/ProcessBuilder, URL/openConnection, ZipInputStream, Random/SecureRandom, path construction and encoder use. I did not inspect every one of the ~1180 Java files in detail; the review focused on trust boundaries, parsers, deserialization and filesystem/network sinks.
limitations: No code was executed and no build/tests/scanners were run; all conclusions are static source reading.
No git history, patches or advisories are available in the snapshot, so I could not confirm which upstream security fix (if any) this revision precedes.
There are no test sources in the snapshot, so security-relevant test evidence (e.g. XXE/deserialization regression tests) could not be consulted.
Platform-level callers of xwiki-commons (XWiki Platform) are out of scope, so attacker reachability for import/filter/status paths is inferred rather than proven.
The P1 index has no data-flow/control-flow and no semantic resolution, and 1 source file is absent from the index; absence of an index fact does not mean the code was reviewed.
Binary-like files are refused/skipped by the tooling; no such files were reported for this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: Netflux WebSocket channel keys, user names and the global history-keeper key are generated with java.util.Random (xwiki-commons-netflux .../internal/Utils.java:40-48; used by Channel.java:36, HistoryKeeper.java:36, NetfluxEndpoint.java:174). The channel key is the only bearer token checked when joining a channel (NetfluxEndpoint.onCommandJoin only checks key length 32/48, lines 242-263) and the history-keeper key unlocks GET_HISTORY for any channel (lines 305-324).
rejected_leads.reason: Real weak-PRNG-for-security-token defect (CWE-338), but exploitation requires recovering java.util.Random seeds across separate instances (nanoTime/seedUniquifier modeling with timing assumptions); I could not corroborate an advisory/CVE or a fix for this specific code, so it was judged a weaker lead than the deserialization issue. Kept as secondary.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultExtensionSerializer.getExtensionElement() parses extension descriptor (XED) XML with a plain DocumentBuilderFactory (no disallow-doctype-decl / external-entity hardening), while sibling code (XMLUtils, tool-xar XMLUtils) does harden parsers.
rejected_leads.reason: Clear XXE-style sink, but in-repo callers pass descriptors from the classpath, the environment and the local extension repository (mostly trusted/app-written); remote XED parsing happens mainly in platform repository code not present here, so attacker control requires a malicious repository/MITM and could not be established from this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtils.parse(LSInput) allows DOCTYPE declarations (disallow-doctype-decl is set to false) while disabling external DTD/entity loading (XMLUtils.java:606-631).
rejected_leads.reason: The parameter values are self-consistent with disabling external entity resolution; without evidence that external entities are actually resolved (or that internal entity expansion is exploitable) this looks like intentional behaviour, not a demonstrable XXE.

rejected_leads.lead: Filter XML input parsing uses a default XMLInputFactory with no SUPPORT_DTD/IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES hardening (XMLInputFilterStreamUtils.java:43, 55-95; StAXUtils.java:53, 118-135).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible XXE/SSRF-in-parser issue, but the effective parser defaults (Woodstox) and the caller context could not be verified from source alone; superseded by the more concrete deserialization sink in the same module.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultJobStatusStore encodes job-id path elements with URLEncoder, which leaves '.' and therefore '..' intact (DefaultJobStatusStore.java:208-225, 341-352); remove() then calls FileUtils.deleteDirectory(jobFolder) (lines 450-469), so a '..' id element would traverse outside the job store.
rejected_leads.reason: Path-traversal-shaped defect, but no caller in this repository passes user-controlled id elements (ids are built by job classes), so attacker control is unproven; FilterStreamConverterJobRequest ids embed serialized filter types (SystemType.unserialize accepts arbitrary strings), which is a possible route, but that chain needs platform callers and was not verified.

rejected_leads.lead: Velocity SecureIntrospector whitelists "getclass" for java.io.File objects (SecureIntrospector.java:106) even though the Class-method whitelist is otherwise restrictive.
rejected_leads.reason: The Class-object whitelist (prepareWhitelistClass) still blocks forName/getClassLoader/newInstance, and Velocity use requires programming rights, which already grant code execution; no escalation chain could be verified, so this was rejected.

rejected_leads.lead: XStream dependency pinned to 1.4.17 (pom.xml:539-543), which predates later XStream security fixes (e.g. 1.4.20).
rejected_leads.reason: Dependency-version issue rather than a source-level defect; also part of the same 'unsafe XStream' theme captured by the main candidate and not independently verifiable here.

summary: Reviewed the xwiki-commons 14.10.3 snapshot (1424 source files; 1186 Java) with the P1 relation index. I surveyed the security-relevant modules (xml, xstream, job, filter, netflux, extension/extension-repositories, velocity, classloader, crypto, cache-infinispan, websocket) and traced sink patterns (XML parsers/DocumentBuilderFactory, XStream usage, Class.forName, Runtime/ProcessBuilder, ZipInputStream, URL/connection handling, Random/SecureRandom, job/extension file-path construction). The strongest plausible issue is the unrestricted XStream XML deserialization path in the filter-stream framework: the XML document itself selects the Java class to instantiate (parameterType/"t" attribute -> Class.forName with initialize=true -> XStream unmarshal/instantiate with no XStream security framework), with the same "no whitelist" design in SafeXStream used for job status / extension history deserialization. Other leads (Netflux channel keys generated with java.util.Random, unhardened DocumentBuilderFactory in the extension serializer, default XMLInputFactory/DOCTYPE handling, URLEncoder-based job-status folder names, XStream 1.4.17 pin) are plausible but weaker/unverified and are listed as rejected leads.
